transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, yes, thank you for seeing me. Um, well, it’s kind of hard to explain, but I guess it really came to a head recently when I was working on a specific project. I'm an artist—I got my bachelor's in fine arts a while ago, so I'm very used to being critical of my own work, you know? It's part of the job. But this was just entirely different. 

I was putting together this memorial piece for my aunt who passed away, and she meant so much to me, so obviously I wanted it to be beautiful and fitting. But instead of just feeling the normal artistic pressure to do a good job, I kept getting these just... awful, really unwanted thoughts that I was going to completely dishonor her somehow. It wasn't just my usual inner critic saying, 'Oh, this composition is a little off.' It was this heavy, terrifying feeling that one wrong photo placement, or even just one slightly wrong color choice, would mean that I didn’t actually love her enough. 

It sounds so irrational saying it out loud, but in the moment, it felt so real and so distressing. Usually, if I have a creative doubt, I just step back from the canvas or the screen, maybe go make some tea, and I can just brush it off and reset. But I couldn’t just brush these thoughts off like normal creative doubts. They just stuck there, making me feel like a terrible niece, and I just couldn't move past them no matter how hard I tried to rationalize with myself. So... yeah, that's why I'm here.
Have you experienced these awful, unwanted thoughts at any other time besides when working on the memorial piece for your aunt?

Um, well, to be completely honest, it’s really that memorial piece that pushed me to finally make an appointment. Like, maybe I’ve had, I don’t know, tiny flashes of being overly perfectionistic about my art in the past? But nothing at all like this. 

Like I was saying, I came in specifically because of what happened with my aunt’s piece. I just kept getting those awful, unwanted thoughts that I was going to completely dishonor her. And I know you're asking about other times, but it's just so hard to even think past this one event because it was so overwhelmingly loud. I would just sit there, staring at the layout on my computer, and my brain would just scream at me that if I moved a photo even a quarter of an inch to the left, or if I picked a shade of green for the background that was slightly too bright, it meant I didn’t love her enough. It was just so heavy, you know? 

And I tried, I really, really tried to just brush them off like my normal creative doubts. I’d tell myself, 'It’s just a color choice, it’s fine, nobody else will even notice,' but I couldn’t. The thoughts just wouldn't budge. They felt so incredibly real and dangerous, like I was committing this terrible crime against her memory just by trying to arrange some pictures. So, yeah, to answer your question, it was really this specific experience that brought me in, because I’ve never been paralyzed like that before, unable to just shake it off and keep working. I just couldn't escape the feeling that I was ruining everything.
Do you often feel overwhelmed by anxiety in situations outside of your artistic work?

Um, outside of my art? No, I don't... I don't think so. Not really. I mean, I think I have a pretty normal amount of stress about, you know, regular life stuff. Like, if I'm running late to meet a friend for coffee, or if I have a big bill coming up and I'm waiting on a client to pay me for a commission—which happens all the time when you're freelancing, let me tell you, the invoicing process can be a total nightmare sometimes. But that's just normal stress, right? Everybody deals with that. It's not... it's not that heavy, paralyzing feeling at all. 

Like, when I'm at the grocery store, I'm just buying groceries. I'm not standing in the produce aisle having a complete meltdown over which apples to buy. I just grab a bag of Honeycrisp and move on with my day. I don't have this screaming voice in my head telling me that if I buy the wrong fruit, it means I'm a terrible person or that I'm dishonoring my family, you know? I just go about my day. I manage my own studio space, I handle my own taxes, I walk my dog, I do all the normal adult things without completely falling apart. 

So it really is just... it's just my art. And honestly, like I was saying, it's specifically that memorial piece. Because even with my regular client work, I can usually just step back and take a breath. But with my aunt's piece, it was just this completely different beast entirely. I keep trying to figure out why *that* specific project triggered such a massive, overwhelming reaction, because normally I'm so put together in my day-to-day life. Why was I sitting at my desk literally crying over the opacity of a drop shadow on a photograph? It just doesn't make any sense to me when the rest of my life is so perfectly manageable. So, yeah, outside of the art... no, I'm honestly fine. It's really just that one specific project that completely derailed me and made me feel so out of control.
When you have these unwanted thoughts, do you feel like they are coming from yourself or do they feel like they are coming from outside of yourself?

Um, they definitely feel like they're coming from me. It's my own brain, my own inner monologue, but it's just... twisted, I guess? Like, I know it's me thinking it. It's not like I'm hearing voices or like someone else is putting the thoughts into my head, if that's what you mean. It's just my own normal thought process getting completely hijacked and turned into this absolute nightmare. 

Like I was saying, that's why I came in, because when I was working on my aunt’s memorial piece, I just kept getting those awful, unwanted thoughts that I was going to dishonor her somehow. And because it's my own brain doing it, it makes it so much harder to fight, you know? Because I'm sitting there, looking at the screen, and it's my own internal voice telling me that one wrong photo placement or one slightly off color choice would mean I didn’t actually love her enough. It's me telling myself that I'm failing her. 

And that's what makes it so incredibly frustrating and distressing. If it were coming from outside, maybe I could just ignore it or tell someone to shut up. But because it's me, it feels like I should be able to control it. But I couldn't. I couldn’t just brush them off like my normal creative doubts. Usually, if my inner critic is being too harsh, I can just tell myself, 'Okay, that's enough, let's look at this objectively.' But with these thoughts about my aunt, it was like my brain was attacking itself, and I was just trapped in the middle of it, completely unable to stop my own mind from convincing me I was doing something terrible. So, yeah, it's definitely me, which honestly just makes the whole thing feel so much worse.
Have you been having these unwanted thoughts about dishonoring your aunt since you finished the memorial piece?

Um, well, finishing it... handing the final file over to the printer was honestly an ordeal in itself. But, since it's been completely done? I mean, like I've been saying, the main reason I even made this appointment was because of what happened *while* I was in the thick of working on it. I just kept getting those awful, unwanted thoughts that I was going to dishonor her somehow. 

And even after it was printed—and my family actually loved it, by the way, my mom was in tears at the memorial service when she saw the display boards, they were printed on this really beautiful matte foam core that didn't catch the glare of the venue lights—but even with all that positive feedback, I just couldn't shake what I went through to get it done. Once the file was locked and sent off, I literally couldn't change the design anymore, so the immediate, screaming panic of 'if this one photo placement is wrong or this color choice is off, it means I didn't love her enough' kind of... shifted? It stopped being about actively making the design choices, because the choices were already set in stone. 

But the memory of it, the weight of it, is still just clinging to me. Because, like I mentioned before, I couldn't just brush them off like my normal creative doubts. Usually, when a project wraps up, I send the final invoice, I close the folder on my desktop, and I feel great. I take a breath and move on to the next client. But this time, I’ve just been sitting in the aftermath of it. It’s like my brain is still exhausted from fighting itself for those three weeks. So, I guess, no, the exact thoughts about moving a picture a quarter-inch aren't happening right this second because the piece is physically finished and out of my hands, but the whole experience of it, the absolute dread that I was somehow betraying her memory... that hasn't really left me at all. It really lingered, which is exactly why I realized I couldn't just ignore it and needed to come talk to someone.
Are you still having those awful, unwanted thoughts about dishonoring your aunt at all, even if they're not as frequent or intense as when you were working on the memorial piece?

Um, well, yes and no? I mean, like I was saying before, the main reason I even came in to see you was because when I was actively working on my aunt’s memorial piece, I just kept getting those awful, unwanted thoughts that I was going to dishonor her somehow. And I know I keep bringing that up, but it really was the catalyst for all of this, and it hasn't entirely let go of me. 

Because even now, with the piece totally finished and sitting in my mom's living room, I still catch myself looking at photos from the memorial service and getting that exact same feeling. Like, my cousin posted a picture online last week, and you could see the display board in the background, and immediately my brain just zoomed right in on it. And it was that exact same thought process all over again—that maybe that one photo placement on the left side was wrong, or maybe the color choice for the background was too cool-toned, and that somehow, making those choices means I didn’t actually love her enough. 

It's just so incredibly frustrating because I really, truly thought that once the printer handed me the physical boards and the event was over, my brain would just turn off and let me rest. But I still can’t just brush them off like my normal creative doubts. Usually, when a project is done, I never think about the font choices or the margins ever again. I just close the book on it. But with this, it's like the echo of those thoughts is still just bouncing around in my head, making me constantly question if I failed her, even though the work is technically over and everyone said it was beautiful. So, yes, they're definitely still there, just... haunting the finished piece instead of the Photoshop file, if that makes any sense? It's just exhausting.
Do these thoughts about dishonoring your aunt feel like they are a part of your own beliefs and values?

Oh, gosh, no. Absolutely not. Honestly, it's the exact opposite, which I think is why it's been so incredibly hard for me to deal with, and why it's been taking up so much space in my head. My aunt and I were so incredibly close, and family is just... it's really paramount to me. My whole personal belief system is about honoring the people I love, and as an artist, I try to do that through my work. So to have my brain constantly telling me that I was doing the exact opposite... it felt like a total betrayal of my own values. 

Like I keep mentioning—and I know I sound like a broken record, but it really is the whole reason I finally made the decision to come in and talk to you—when I was working on that memorial piece, I just kept getting bombarded by these awful, completely unwanted thoughts that I was going to dishonor her somehow. And it wasn't just a passing worry, it was this heavy, crushing feeling that if I made one wrong photo placement, or if the color choice was even slightly off, it literally meant I didn't love her enough. 

And my actual values, my real beliefs, they tell me that love isn't measured by a hex code or a margin width, you know? I know that logically. I know my aunt knew how much I loved her, and she would have loved anything I made. But the thoughts just wouldn't align with that reality, and I couldn't just brush them off like my normal creative doubts. Usually, if a design isn't working, I can just say, 'Oh, this composition doesn't reflect my style,' and fix it without a second thought. But this felt like it was attacking my actual character, my actual love for her, and twisting it into something ugly. So, no, they don't feel like my real beliefs at all. They feel like this weird, twisted funhouse mirror version of what I actually care about, which is just... it's just really upsetting to deal with.
Do you find yourself having these unwanted thoughts about dishonoring your aunt on a daily basis?

Every single day? Um... yeah, honestly, I would say it’s pretty much a daily thing at this point. Or, at the very least, it absolutely was every single day when I was in the thick of the project, and the echoes of it are still happening daily now. 

I know I keep circling back to this exact same point, and I really am sorry if I’m just repeating myself over and over, but it just... it really is the entire reason I finally made this appointment in the first place. Because when I was actually in the middle of working on my aunt’s memorial piece, it wasn't just an occasional worry that popped up once a week. It was an everyday, constant barrage of these awful, completely unwanted thoughts that I was going to dishonor her somehow. I’d wake up, go to the kitchen to make my morning coffee—I usually do a pour-over, which takes a few minutes of just standing there pouring the water, right? And usually that’s my quiet time to just breathe and ease into the morning. But instead, my brain would just immediately start in on me before I even had my first sip, telling me that if the photo placement on one of the display boards was wrong, or if the color choice for the typography wasn't perfectly respectful, it literally meant I didn't actually love her enough. 

And it’s just so exhausting to deal with that every single day. Because, like I’ve been saying, I couldn't just brush them off like my normal creative doubts. Normally, if I doubt a design on a Tuesday, by Wednesday I’ve tweaked the layout, sent off a new proof, and moved on, and I don't think about it again. But this was day in, day out, just this relentless feeling of dread that I was doing something unforgivable. And even now, on a daily basis... yeah, I still get those flashes. I'll just be driving to the grocery store or sitting at my desk opening up Illustrator for a totally different, unrelated client, and boom, the thought is just there again, weighing on me and making my chest tight all over again. So, yes, daily is probably the most accurate way to describe it.
Are these daily unwanted thoughts about dishonoring your aunt affecting your ability to do other things you normally enjoy or daily tasks outside of your art?

Um, well... I guess I’d say I’m still functioning, for the most part? Like, I’m still getting most of my actual client work done, eventually, because, you know, I have to pay my rent and keep the lights on. But it’s... it’s the ripple effect of it all that’s really starting to take a toll on the rest of my life. 

Because, like I was saying, these thoughts are just so heavy and so completely exhausting. When I go into my workspace now, even if I’m sitting down to work on a completely unrelated branding package for a client, I end up losing so much time. I’ll just be sitting there at my desk, staring at my monitor, completely paralyzed by this lingering dread about my aunt’s memorial piece, just trying to convince myself over and over that I didn't somehow ruin her memory with a bad design choice. 

And all that extra time I lose in the studio just sitting there, fighting with my own brain... it really adds up. It actually already cost me a grant deadline last month. It was this local arts council grant that I usually apply for, and it requires a lot of writing and organizing portfolio pieces. But because I was just so mentally drained from trying to get through my regular workday while dealing with these thoughts, I kept pushing the application off, and then I just completely missed the submission window. Which is so incredibly unlike me! I’m usually very on top of my administrative stuff. 

And it’s not just the business side of things, either. It’s affecting things I actually really enjoy doing. There was this gallery talk I was scheduled to do a couple of weeks ago—just a small local event, talking about my creative process with a few other artists. And I had actually really wanted to do it. I usually love connecting with the community like that and talking about design. But as the date got closer, I just... I couldn't do it. My head was just so loud with all this guilt and these awful thoughts, and I felt like such a total fraud trying to go up there and talk about the joy of creating art when my own art was the exact thing making me feel like a terrible person. So I ended up having to back out at the last minute and make up some excuse to the organizer about feeling under the weather. 

So, yeah, I mean, I’m technically still getting by and keeping my head above water with my main job, but it’s definitely bleeding over and stealing away opportunities and things that I actually really value.
Are these unwanted thoughts about dishonoring your aunt interfering with your relationships with friends or family?

Um... no, actually. I wouldn't say they're interfering with my relationships. I mean, not that I've noticed anyway. My friends and family have actually been incredibly supportive through all of this, even if they don't fully understand exactly what's going on in my head. 

Like, just this past weekend, my younger sister and I met up for dinner at this little Italian place downtown—she's absolutely obsessed with their mushroom risotto, so we go there probably twice a month—and we just sat there and talked for like three hours. And, you know, I didn't even bring up all the stuff about the memorial piece or the thoughts I've been having, mostly because I just didn't want to bring down the mood and make the whole dinner about my stress, but she knows I've been having a hard time and she was just so great to be around. 

And my friends from art school, we have this group chat that is honestly constantly going off, just pinging all day with memes and design inspiration and life updates. I might be a little bit slower to reply sometimes, especially if I'm having a bad morning and I'm just stuck staring at my monitor feeling that heavy dread I was talking about earlier, but I'm still talking to them. I'm still showing up. If anything, I think I almost cling to those relationships a bit more right now because they kind of ground me, you know? 

Like, my mom calls me every single Sunday morning without fail, and we just talk about her garden or whatever historical fiction book she's reading for her book club, and it's just... it's really nice to just be a daughter and a friend and not just a person trapped in a spiral about a design project. I haven't really told my mom the full extent of these thoughts, obviously, because she's still actively grieving my aunt too, and I would never, ever want to add to her plate right now. But our relationship is still really solid. 

So, yeah, I guess internally I might be a little more distracted when I'm hanging out with people, because part of my brain is still chewing on whether I used the right typeface on that display board, but the relationships themselves? No, they're completely fine. They haven't been damaged by this or anything like that.
Are these unwanted thoughts about dishonoring your aunt causing you significant distress or interfering with your daily life in any way?

Um, yeah, absolutely. I know I kind of spilled a lot of this just a minute ago, so forgive me if I'm repeating myself, but yes, the distress is... it's really, really significant. It's just this heavy, constant weight that sits right on my chest. 

And as far as interfering with my daily life... well, like I was saying before, I am still technically functioning, right? I’m still getting most of my actual client work done, eventually, because I have deadlines and I have to pay my rent, and I've always been a very responsible person when it comes to my career. But it’s the sheer amount of extra time I lose just sitting there in my studio. I'll just be staring blankly at my screen, totally frozen, trying to fight off these thoughts and convince myself I'm not a terrible person who ruined her aunt's memory. 

And that lost time has real, tangible consequences. Like I mentioned earlier about that local arts council grant—I completely missed the deadline because I was just too mentally drained from battling my own brain all day to put my portfolio pieces together. And having to back out of that gallery talk... I mean, I really, really had wanted to do that. It was supposed to be this wonderful evening talking about creative processes with other local artists, and I had my whole presentation practically outlined in my head weeks in advance, but I just couldn't bring myself to stand up there feeling like such a fraud. 

So, even though I'm keeping my head above water with my main job, it's definitely stealing away these other important opportunities and causing me a lot of grief in the process. It's just so incredibly frustrating to watch myself miss out on these things I actually care about, just because I can't get these thoughts to stop.
Do you feel like these thoughts about dishonoring your aunt are in line with your own identity and self-image?

Oh, gosh, no. Not at all. Honestly, that’s exactly why I finally decided I needed to come in and talk to someone in the first place. Because it just feels so completely foreign to who I am. 

I mean, I have my degree in this, I’ve been working as a professional designer for years, so I am very, very used to second-guessing myself. Normal creative doubts are just part of the job, you know? You sit there and wonder, 'Is this typeface too heavy?' or 'Does this layout actually make sense?' and you tweak it and move on. 

But when I was working on my aunt’s memorial piece... it wasn't like that at all. It wasn't my normal artistic process. I just kept getting these awful, completely unwanted thoughts that I was going to dishonor her somehow. And it was so extreme. It was this intense feeling that like, one wrong photo placement, or one slightly off color choice would actually mean that I didn’t love her enough. Which is just so incredibly far from the truth, because I loved her dearly! She was such a wonderful person and we were so close. 

So to sit there and have my own brain try to convince me that picking the wrong shade of blue or cropping a picture a certain way means I'm disrespecting her entire legacy... it just goes against everything I know about myself and my relationship with her. And usually, like I said, I can just push through a creative block. I can tell my inner critic to quiet down and just get the work done. But with this, I couldn’t just brush them off like normal creative doubts. They just lodged themselves in my head and made me feel like an absolute monster over a simple design choice. So, no, it really doesn't feel like me at all. It feels completely against my nature, which is why it's been so terrifying.
Are you avoiding certain activities or situations because of these unwanted thoughts about dishonoring your aunt?

Um... no, actually. I don't think I'm avoiding anything, really. I mean, not outside of the things I already mentioned, like backing out of that gallery talk and missing the grant deadline because I was just too exhausted from dealing with all of this in my head. But as far as actively avoiding things *because* of the thoughts? No. 

I'm still going to my studio every day. I'm still opening up my design software, even though sometimes just looking at the Adobe Illustrator loading screen makes my stomach do this horrible little flip because it reminds me of when I was working on the memorial piece. But I still do it. I still sit down at my desk, I still make my morning coffee—usually a pour-over, which takes a few minutes and kind of gives me a chance to just breathe before I look at my monitor—and I still get to work on my current client projects. 

Like right now, I'm doing a full branding package for this new boutique bakery opening up in the West End, and I'm still doing all the mockups and the logo designs for them. I'm not avoiding design work or avoiding being creative. And I'm definitely not avoiding my family or anything related to my aunt. I actually went over to my uncle's house last week to help him sort through some of her old gardening tools, because she had this incredible collection of vintage trowels and things that he didn't know what to do with. And being there, in her space, it didn't trigger those specific thoughts about dishonoring her. 

It really just seems to be centered around that one specific project and the memory of working on it, rather than making me want to run away from my life or my work in general. So, yeah, I'm still doing all my normal activities, just... carrying this heavy, exhausting mental weight while I do them.
Have these unwanted thoughts about dishonoring your aunt been affecting your sleep?

Um, my sleep? No, I wouldn't say so. Not really, anyway. I mean, I still get my usual, you know, seven or eight hours most nights. I’ve always been someone who needs a solid amount of sleep to function creatively the next day. If I don't get at least seven hours, my brain just feels like mush and I can't even pick out a decent color palette, let alone design a whole branding package. 

So, I’m pretty strict about my nighttime routine. I usually try to wind down around 10:30, maybe read a little bit—right now I'm reading this fascinating biography of this mid-century textile designer, it's really inspiring—and then I'm usually asleep by 11:30. And once I'm asleep, I'm out. I don't really wake up in the middle of the night tossing and turning or anything like that. 

Sure, sometimes when I'm first lying there in the dark, my mind might wander a bit, and those thoughts about the memorial piece might sort of drift in, just because it’s quiet and there aren't any distractions. But it's not keeping me awake for hours or causing insomnia. It's more just... daytime exhaustion. Like I said before, battling these thoughts all day while I'm at my desk is just so incredibly draining that by the time evening rolls around, I'm honestly just ready to crash. My body is just done. So, if anything, I might actually be falling asleep a little faster than usual just because I'm so mentally fatigued from the whole ordeal. But the sleep itself? No, it's been pretty normal, thankfully. I think if I were losing sleep on top of everything else, I'd really be a wreck.
Do you feel compelled to repeat certain behaviors or rituals as a result of these unwanted thoughts about dishonoring your aunt?

Well, yes, actually. That's... that's a big part of what makes it all so exhausting. It’s not just the thoughts themselves, it’s what I feel like I have to do to make them stop, or at least make them quiet down for a little bit. 

Like, when I was working on that memorial piece for my aunt, and even now when I'm setting up a display or working on a layout... if that thought pops into my head that I'm somehow disrespecting her or doing it wrong, I can't just let it go. I get stuck. So, for example, if I'm arranging objects on a table for a still life reference, or even just organizing my own desk, I’ll end up nudging the same objects over and over. Just moving a pen a millimeter to the left, then a millimeter to the right, trying to find the exact spot where it feels... I don't know, 'settled.' 

And it’s the same with the design work itself. I will sit there and reread the same small block of label text on a mockup ten, fifteen, twenty times. Just reading the exact same words, making sure I didn't miss a typo that would somehow ruin the whole thing and make me a terrible person. Or I'll check the layout photos over and over again. I'll zoom in on the edges, check the alignment, zoom out, check it again, open a different file, go back and check the first one again. 

And the worst part is, the logical, professional designer part of my brain is sitting there the whole time going, 'What are you doing? This is perfectly aligned. You checked this an hour ago. It's fine.' I know it's fine! I know I'm just wasting precious studio time. I mean, I have deadlines, I have clients waiting on proofs, and instead of moving forward, I'm stuck in this loop of checking and adjusting and rereading. But I just... I can't stop until that internal feeling of dread sort of dissipates and my brain finally gives me the green light that it feels 'right.' It’s incredibly frustrating because I know I'm doing it, but I feel completely compelled to keep doing it anyway.
Are these unwanted thoughts about dishonoring your aunt causing you a lot of emotional pain?

Emotional pain? Um... I don't know if I'd call it *pain*, exactly. Not like, you know, not like the grief when she actually passed away, which was this sharp, agonizing thing where I couldn't breathe. This is different. It's more of just a... a really profound discomfort and exhaustion. 

I mean, I definitely feel distressed by it. It's horrible feeling like I'm somehow doing a disservice to her memory when all I wanted to do was honor her. My aunt was the one who first taught me how to mix watercolors when I was like, seven years old, sitting at her kitchen table with those little plastic palettes. So the idea that I'm disrespecting her is really upsetting to me. But it's not so much a sharp emotional pain as it is this dull, heavy, persistent feeling of being totally worn down. 

It’s like, when I'm stuck in that loop of checking the alignment on a design file for the twentieth time, I'm not sitting there crying or feeling heartbroken. I'm just feeling incredibly frustrated and trapped. It's this tense, tight feeling in my chest, like a coiled spring, just waiting for the moment when my brain finally decides it's "right" so I can move on. So, yeah, it's definitely distressing and it makes me feel terrible, but "emotional pain" feels like a slightly different category than what I'm actually experiencing on a day-to-day basis with all this. It's more of a mental fatigue and a deep, deep frustration with myself.
Do you feel significant anxiety when these unwanted thoughts about dishonoring your aunt occur?

Anxiety? Um, no, I wouldn't really use that word. I mean, I know what anxiety feels like. When I was in art school, leading up to my senior thesis exhibition, I was a complete wreck. My heart would pound, my palms would get sweaty, I'd feel this sort of fluttery panic in my stomach every time I thought about the critiques. I was so anxious I could barely eat. But this? This isn't like that at all. 

When the thoughts happen, it's not a panicky feeling. It's more of that... that tension I was talking about. That heavy, frustrating feeling where I just feel compelled to fix it. Like, if I'm looking at a mockup and the thought pops in that I've used a font that my aunt would have hated, or that the kerning is somehow an insult to her memory—which sounds ridiculous out loud, I know, but that's what happens—I don't get a racing heart or shortness of breath. I just get this immediate, overwhelming sense of... of wrongness. 

It's just this intense, nagging pressure that I have to adjust it right now. And I'll sit there, staring at the screen, clicking the mouse, nudging the text box, just feeling really, really stuck. But I'm not sitting there trembling or feeling afraid, you know? It's not fear. It's just this incredibly stubborn, exhausting need to make the feeling of wrongness go away so I can just get back to work. So, yeah, I really wouldn't call it anxiety. It's just incredibly draining.
Have these unwanted thoughts about dishonoring your aunt persisted since our last discussion?

Well, I mean... since our last discussion? I'm trying to think back to exactly when that was, but honestly, my days kind of blur together lately with all the time I spend in the studio. But if you're asking if the thoughts are still there... yeah. They definitely are. 

It's not like they ever really went away, you know? It's just this constant, low-level hum in the background of my brain whenever I'm working on anything remotely connected to her, or even just when I'm trying to set up my workspace. Like yesterday, I was pulling out some old sketchbooks, just trying to find some inspiration for a new commission—this really lovely floral pattern for a boutique's packaging, actually—and I saw a doodle I did years ago that reminded me of her. And immediately, that thought was right there again. Just, 'Are you sure you're honoring her? Are you sure you're not somehow tarnishing her memory by using this technique she taught you for a commercial project?' 

And then I'm off, right back into it. So, yes, they've persisted. I wouldn't say they've gotten wildly out of control or anything, I'm still getting my work done eventually, but they haven't stopped. It's just... it's just always there, waiting for me to sit down at my drafting table or open Illustrator. I keep hoping I'll wake up one day and just be able to design a memorial piece or organize my pens without my brain turning it into this whole... ordeal about respect and dishonor. But so far, no luck with that. They're definitely still hanging around, just as stubborn as ever.
Do you feel like you have to perform any specific rituals or behaviors to try to get rid of these unwanted thoughts about dishonoring your aunt?

Well, I mean, "rituals" makes it sound like I'm lighting candles or chanting or something, which I'm definitely not doing. But if you mean, do I have to *do* things to make that heavy, wrong feeling go away? Then, yeah. Absolutely. It's like I was saying before with the design files, but it happens with physical stuff, too. 

Like, if I'm setting up a still life to paint, and I'm using this antique silver creamer that actually belonged to her—she gave it to me when I moved into my first apartment—I'll place it on the table.
